J: Sitting out there, I feel a mix of pride and protectiveness. Pride because you can hear three languages at once, kids weaving between plots, someone sharing mint for tea with a neighbor they just met. Protectiveness because shared spaces only work if we all treat them right. I’m friendly first, but I like clear house rules everyone can see.

Day to day, I start simple: eye contact, a hello, names. “I’m Jess from the blue house—take some tomatoes, we’ve got too many.” I don’t need anyone’s life story to be a good neighbor. If we can swap recipes or tools, even better. If we don’t share words, we’ve got smiles, hand gestures, and a translation app. I’ll put signs up in a couple languages and with pictures—please don’t pick from someone else’s plot, no glass, keep dogs leashed.

Differences don’t scare me; disrespect does. I don’t care who you love, how you pray, or what your family looks like—that’s your business. What matters in the garden is behavior: clean up after yourself, keep the music to a reasonable hour, say something if you break a tool, and check on folks when it’s 100 degrees out. We’re all using the same hose.

When someone’s struggling—say, with drinking or using—I try to lead with care but hold a line. I’ll offer a bottle of water, a chair in the shade, a number for local help if they’re open to it. But I won’t look the other way on broken glass or unsafe stuff in a place where kids play. Same with health issues: I follow basic hygiene, don’t gossip about anyone’s condition, and I won’t let fear turn into exclusion. If there’s a concern, we handle it privately and respectfully, with real info, not rumors.

Cultural mix-ups happen. If a family throws late-night parties and it’s keeping folks up, I’ll walk over with a plate and say, “Hey, love that you’re celebrating—could we wrap by 10 on weeknights?” Nine times out of ten, it’s fine once you actually talk. If it keeps happening, we bring it to the group and set a clear quiet-hours agreement. Same rule for everyone.

Language can be a hurdle, not a wall. Kids are great bridges—they’ll show you how to say hello better than any app. We can post a sheet with pictures for shared tasks, start a group chat with a couple volunteer translators, and do a seed swap or workday where talking is optional—hands busy, smiles do the rest.

I’m big on “take a turn.” Water on Tuesdays, weed the path once a month, bring a dish to the potluck if you can—store-bought is fine. If you’re new or shy, I’ll pair you with someone who’s been around so you know how things run. Accountability doesn’t have to be mean; it just has to be even.

Bottom line: open door, clear rules. Help first, judge last. That’s the kind of community I want to sit in and wave at all afternoon.

Here’s how I’d handle it in the garden and on the block:

- Baseline we all agree to: no harassing or slurs, don’t touch other people’s stuff without permission, clean up your area, keep noise to agreed quiet hours, and keep kids’ spaces safe. Same rules for everyone, enforced the same way.

- Different backgrounds don’t need different rules—just a little extra care in how we interact. I make a point to greet people by name, learn a hello in their language, and use signs with pictures plus a couple languages. We label potluck dishes for dietary needs and try not to schedule noisy events on big religious holidays. If I mess up, I say so and fix it.

When folks are struggling with alcohol or drugs:
- Lead with care, hold a line. I’ll offer water, shade, and a seat, and quietly share a list of local support numbers if they want it. But I won’t ignore unsafe behavior—no open containers in kids’ areas, no glass, no leaving paraphernalia around. If there’s a risk (like needles), we set up a sealed sharps container and a clear “what to do if you find one” note. If someone is a danger to themselves or others, we pause the activity and call appropriate help. Reason: kids and elders use this space. Dignity and safety both matter.

When it comes to health and infectious illnesses:
- Respect privacy, follow basic hygiene. We keep sanitizer by the tools, wipe handles after use, and don’t gossip about anyone’s medical situation. If there’s a specific concern, we look up guidance from the local health department and stick to facts, not rumors. No shaming people for conditions they may have; we just keep shared spaces clean.

Across race, religion, and language:
- Assume good intent first. If music’s blasting at 11 on a Tuesday, I’ll walk over with a plate and say, “Love the party—could we wrap by 10 on weeknights?” Usually that solves it. If not, we bring it to the group and set a clear, posted quiet-hours rule. We add simple translation help—volunteer buddies, picture-based signs, and patience. Eye-rolling at accents or “speak English” comments? That gets shut down—kindly but firmly. Reason: people stick around and contribute when they’re respected; they shut down when they’re mocked.

Sexual orientation and family structure:
- Not my business unless it affects behavior in the shared space, which it doesn’t. Cohabiting, married, straight, gay—same expectations: pitch in, be respectful. No prying questions, no jokes at someone’s expense. If I hear something snide, I’ll say, “We don’t do that here.” Reason: folks have long memories for being judged; a little decency goes a long way toward everyone feeling safe.

Where we need more communication and tolerance:
- Noise and celebrations: different cultures party differently. We set quiet hours and a simple “heads-up” thread so big gatherings don’t blindside anyone.
- Food smells and grilling: agree on times and locations; if someone’s fasting or has restrictions, we label food and keep a veggie option around.
- Kids and mess: kids will be kids. We set “clean-up together” times and chalk out play zones so tomatoes don’t get trampled.
- Dogs: leash, scoop, and keep out of beds. Post it clearly.
- Smoking/vaping: a designated spot away from kids and crops, or not allowed at all if that’s the group’s choice—decide it together and stick to it.
- Health worries: facts beat fear. We post basic hygiene steps and avoid talking about people’s private medical stuff.

Practical setups that help:
- A one-page “house rules” with pictures, in a couple languages.
- A quick orientation for new folks—pair them with a neighbor for their first workday.
- A resource board: food pantry hours, addiction support, tenant help, free clinic info.
- Conflict steps: talk one-on-one first, then small group, then a group decision if it keeps happening. Start with a friendly reminder; repeat issues get consequences everyone agreed to.

Why this works: Most blowups aren’t about values; they’re about not knowing the norms, feeling disrespected, or carrying stress from elsewhere. Clear, even rules plus a little human grace cover 90% of it. The rest needs steady boundaries—same for me as for you. Help first, judge last. That’s how you make a space where a lot of different people can actually relax next to each other.

- Respect privacy, follow basic hygiene. We keep sanitizer by the tools, wipe handles after use, and don’t gossip about anyone’s medical situation. If there’s a specific concern, we look up guidance from the local health department and stick to facts, not rumors. No shaming people for conditions they may have; we just keep shared spaces clean.

Across race, religion, and language:
- Assume good intent first. If music’s blasting at 11 on a Tuesday, I’ll walk over with a plate and say, “Love the party—could we wrap by 10 on weeknights?” Usually that solves it. If not, we bring it to the group and set a clear, posted quiet-hours rule. We add simple translation help—volunteer buddies, picture-based signs, and patience. Eye-rolling at accents or “speak English” comments? That gets shut down—kindly but firmly. Reason: people stick around and contribute when they’re respected; they shut down when they’re mocked.

Sexual orientation and family structure:
- Not my business unless it affects behavior in the shared space, which it doesn’t. Cohabiting, married, straight, gay—same expectations: pitch in, be respectful. No prying questions, no jokes at someone’s expense. If I hear something snide, I’ll say, “We don’t do that here.” Reason: folks have long memories for being judged; a little decency goes a long way toward everyone feeling safe.

Where we need more communication and tolerance:
- Noise and celebrations: different cultures party differently. We set quiet hours and a simple “heads-up” thread so big gatherings don’t blindside anyone.
- Food smells and grilling: agree on times and locations; if someone’s fasting or has restrictions, we label food and keep a veggie option around.
- Kids and mess: kids will be kids. We set “clean-up together” times and chalk out play zones so tomatoes don’t get trampled.
- Dogs: leash, scoop, and keep out of beds. Post it clearly.
- Smoking/vaping: a designated spot away from kids and crops, or not allowed at all if that’s the group’s choice—decide it together and stick to it.
- Health worries: facts beat fear. We post basic hygiene steps and avoid talking about people’s private medical stuff.

Practical setups that help:
- A one-page “house rules” with pictures, in a couple languages.
- A quick orientation for new folks—pair them with a neighbor for their first workday.
- A resource board: food pantry hours, addiction support, tenant help, free clinic info.
- Conflict steps: talk one-on-one first, then small group, then a group decision if it keeps happening. Start with a friendly reminder; repeat issues get consequences everyone agreed to.

Why this works: Most blowups aren’t about values; they’re about not knowing the norms, feeling disrespected, or carrying stress from elsewhere. Clear, even rules plus a little human grace cover 90% of it. The rest needs steady boundaries—same for me as for you. Help first, judge last. That’s how you make a space where a lot of different people can actually relax next to each other.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character10_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
J: When jobs are tight, fairness to me is two-sided: locals shouldn’t be pushed out or undercut, and migrants shouldn’t be used up and tossed aside. Same rules, same pay, same protections—whoever’s wearing the apron or hard hat.

I learned this watching hours get cut at the store while a contractor brought in a cash crew for cheaper. You can’t blame people for taking work; you have to fix the incentives and hold employers to the line.

Here’s how I’d balance it:

- Local-first at a fair wage: Post the job publicly, offer a decent rate with normal benefits, and give locals a real shot. If after a set time you still can’t fill it, then open it to migrant workers. Reason: a lot of folks can do the work if the pay and schedule aren’t rock-bottom.

- Equal pay for equal work: No “discount” labor. If a job goes to a migrant worker, the wage should match or be a hair above the going rate so you’re proving a true shortage, not just shaving costs. Reason: stops undercutting and wage races to the bottom.

- Enforce the basics: Crack down on wage theft, off-the-books pay, unsafe worksites. Fine the employers, not just the workers trying to get by. Use simple tools like ID checks and payroll audits, not gotcha raids. Reason: bad bosses create most of the unfairness.

- Train our own while welcoming help: Put a slice of work-permit fees into local training—apprenticeships, CDL programs, childcare and bus passes so people can actually take those jobs. Reason: sometimes it’s not skill, it’s barriers like childcare or transport.

- Numbers that flex with the economy: Tie work visa slots to local unemployment and real labor data, and adjust by region. Seasonal work should have seasonal caps and clear start/stop dates. Reason: one-size-fits-all doesn’t match how towns actually live.

- Portable status and safety: If migrants come to fill a shortage, make the work permit portable so they can switch employers without risking deportation. Give them the same safety protections and a clean way to report abuse. Reason: if your boss owns your status, you can’t say no to exploitation.

- Community give-back: Big employers who bring in outside labor should chip into local funds—housing, clinic hours, school capacity—so the neighborhood isn’t carrying all the costs alone. Reason: growth is fine if you help pay for the strain it brings.

- Clear, humane borders: Have orderly legal paths and stick to them. Focus enforcement on fraud and exploitation, not on families just trying to keep a roof over their heads. Due process, no midnight rule changes. Reason: fairness means predictable rules.

- Transparency and voice: Publish the data—how many hires were local, how many permits issued, wages paid. Hold a town hall twice a year so folks can flag problems and suggest fixes. Reason: people accept trade-offs better when they aren’t kept in the dark.

Bottom line: give locals a fair first shot and the tools to step up, and bring in migrant workers where the need is real—while making sure everyone plays by the same rulebook. That’s the balance that feels right to me: level the field, protect the person, and put the weight where it belongs—on employers to do it right.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character10_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
J: Big picture, I think a lot of people are talking about real things, but they’re talking past each other. Here’s how it sorts in my head:

- Filling vital roles: True in plenty of sectors—farm work, elder care, some trades, seasonal gigs. But “shortage” should mean you posted the job at a fair wage with decent hours and still couldn’t fill it. If you can’t raise pay a dollar but can bus people in, that’s not a shortage, that’s a choice.

- Cultural diversity and vitality: I see the upside—food, music, new small businesses, kids growing up comfortable with difference. It works best when we have shared “house rules” (basic laws, norms, English-learning support) so the mix doesn’t turn into silos.

- Security and crime fears: I get why people worry; news makes scary stuff loud. From what I’ve seen in the data and in life, most immigrants come to work and keep their heads down, and they’re not more crime-prone than locals. Real risks exist—trafficking, bad actors—but they’re best handled with targeted enforcement and going after exploitative employers, not blanket suspicion.

- Terrorism: The risk is not zero, but it’s rare, and refugee vetting is already intense. Focus resources where they matter—intelligence, trafficking rings—while keeping everyday life from turning into theater.

- Humanitarian cases: I support taking in refugees and people fleeing real danger—clear criteria, due process, and proper support so towns aren’t left alone to figure it out. If the federal government places folks, there should be funding for schools, housing, and clinics to match.

- Jobs and wages pressure: This is felt most by workers like me. The answer isn’t blaming migrants—it’s stopping employers from using them to undercut. Equal pay for equal work, enforce labor laws, make work permits portable, and invest in training/childcare/transport so locals can step into openings.

Where I want more receipts and dialogue:
- Local labor data: Were jobs truly posted at a fair wage? How long? What changed when pay/conditions improved?
- Wage impacts: Break it out by sector and region—who’s actually losing ground, who’s gaining?
- Housing and services: How much strain on rents, classrooms, ERs—and what funding follows new arrivals?
- Crime and safety: Regular, transparent stats by offense and status, so we’re arguing facts, not headlines.
- Integration outcomes: English access, school outcomes for kids, time-to-earning a living wage—what works, what doesn’t?

What sounds reasonable to me:
- Legal, orderly pathways tied to real needs.
- Strong labor enforcement that lands on bosses, not on workers trying to eat.
- Community support where numbers are rising—paid for by the levels of government making the policy and by big employers benefiting.
- A cap that flexes with the economy, with room for emergencies (wars, disasters).

What needs careful pushback:
- Blanket claims that immigrants cause crime or “take all the jobs.” Show me the numbers and the wages offered.
- “Open borders” with no plan for housing, schools, or worksite enforcement. That’s not fair to anyone—newcomers or locals.

Bottom line: I’m for a system that’s predictable, humane, and honest about trade-offs. Bring people in where there’s real need, protect all workers the same, and publish the receipts so communities can see it’s on the level. That’s how you get buy-in from folks like me.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character10_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
J: I’m not for “let everybody in” and I’m not for “shut the door.” Both feel unfair and unworkable. I’d pick a middle lane: admit people based on real job need, with numerical limits that flex with the economy, plus a steady humanitarian lane. Clear rules, same protections for everyone, honest about capacity.

What I’d back:

- Job-demand plus a wage test:
  - Post locally first at a fair wage. If it’s still unfilled after, say, 30 days, open it to work visas.
  - Set a wage floor at or above the prevailing rate (even a bit higher) to prove it’s a true shortage, not cheap-labor hunting.
  - Permits should be portable so a worker can leave a bad boss without losing status.

- Caps that flex:
  - National and regional caps tied to unemployment and real labor data, reviewed quarterly.
  - Seasonal caps for farm/hospitality with clear start/stop dates.

- Shared costs, shared benefits:
  - Employers bringing in outside labor chip into local funds for housing, schools, and clinics.
  - Real penalties for wage theft and unsafe worksites; repeat offenders lose the right to sponsor anyone.

- Local-first support:
  - Use a slice of permit fees for training, apprenticeships, childcare, and transport so locals can step into openings.
  - Publicly post hiring stats—how many locals hired, wages paid—so folks can see it’s on the level.

- Humanitarian lane:
  - Keep a steady, vetted path for refugees/asylum seekers, with federal dollars following placements so towns aren’t left holding the bag.

- Family unity, with limits:
  - Allow close family sponsorship with reasonable caps and a clear timeline, plus an orientation so newcomers know the “house rules.”

- Integration basics:
  - English classes, credential help, and a simple orientation to laws, work norms, and community expectations.

Why not the other options:
- Complete openness: housing, schools, and wages would get whiplash. That’s not fair to newcomers or the neighborhoods they land in.
- Total refusal: we’d hobble farms, elder care, and a bunch of small businesses—and push work into the shadows where abuse grows.

Bottom line: open door, clear rules. Let people in where the need is proven, protect all workers the same, and make sure the community has what it needs to absorb change. That’s the balance that feels fair and keeps the peace.

J: Stepping in as her sharpened a few things for me.

So yes—I understand her better, and I think my own views got more practical. If we keep her voice in the room—help first, judge last, same rules for all—we’ll make better choices and better neighbors.

I remember after that big storm a few years back, all the neighbors came out, sharing food and helping each other. That’s what community means to me: pitching in, knowing you have someone’s back, and not just thinking about yourself. It’s not perfect, but it’s worth fighting for.

You get to meet folks with totally different stories, and sometimes you learn something new. It can bring a bit of life to a place that might otherwise feel stuck. I’ve had good chats with people who weren’t born here, or who have different ways of doing things. That’s interesting to me.

But I’d be lying if I said it was always easy or comfortable. Sometimes I feel kind of awkward, especially if there’s a language barrier, or if I don’t understand their traditions or where they’re coming from. There’s moments I worry about saying the wrong thing or not knowing how to act. And sometimes, I wonder if they feel the same about me.

Still, I think if everyone’s open and willing to listen, it can work. For me, it matters that people respect each other: follow the basic rules, help each other out, don’t make others feel unwelcome. I’m not someone who thinks you have to give up your background to fit in, but I do think you have to try and be a good neighbor. That means making an effort—both ways. If we can do that, it’s worth having all these different people in the same community.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. I also think it’s important to look out for refugees or those facing real danger where they’re from. Maybe set aside a part of the quota for humanitarian reasons, but make sure we have programs to help those folks adjust, learn English, and find work, so they can actually become part of the community.

Integration matters. So, I’d want policies that not only control numbers, but also help new arrivals get settled and mix with locals, instead of just living separate lives. That helps avoid tension and makes it easier for everyone—old-timers and newcomers—to feel like they belong.

So for me, balancing fairness and social integration means: bring people in when there’s a real need, make sure the numbers make sense for the community, and give support to help everyone get along. That feels fair, practical, and like the right thing to do.

Maybe there's room for guest worker programs or something, where it's all above board and regulated. But this current system where everything's under the table? It's not fair to anyone - not to us, not to them, not to their families.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character10_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, looking thoughtful*

You know, I think most of these perspectives have some truth to them, which is what makes this whole thing so complicated.

*counting on fingers*

The labor shortage argument - I can see that in some areas. Farms need workers, hospitals need nurses. But I also see it being used to justify bringing in workers when there are still Americans looking for those jobs. Maybe the real issue is that some jobs don't pay enough to attract local workers? Instead of importing cheaper labor, maybe we should be asking why those wages are so low.

*speaking more cautiously*

The cultural diversity thing... look, I've enjoyed trying new foods and learning about different traditions. But I also think there's value in having some shared culture that binds us together as Americans. When whole neighborhoods become like little foreign countries where English isn't spoken, that worries me. Not because other cultures are bad, but because we need some common ground.

*voice becoming more serious*

The security concerns - I think those are legitimate and shouldn't be dismissed as racism. We need to know who's coming in. That's just common sense. Maybe the numbers about crime are debated, but even if it's not a huge increase, shouldn't we be preventing any preventable crimes?

*softening*

The humanitarian side... my heart does go out to people fleeing real persecution. But I think we need to be honest about our capacity. We can't save everyone, and trying to might hurt the people who are already here struggling.

*pausing*

I guess what frustrates me is that anyone who questions immigration gets called heartless or racist, when really I just want policies that work for everyone - including the Americans who are barely hanging on.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character10_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leaning back, considering carefully*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. I mean, we can't handle everyone who wants to come - our schools are already overcrowded, our healthcare system is strained, and there aren't enough good jobs for the people already here. That would be chaos.

*speaking more decisively*

I think we need a combination approach, but with some clear priorities. First, we need to drastically reduce the numbers for a while - give communities like mine time to catch up, let wages rise, let our kids compete for jobs without being undercut.

*warming to the topic*

When we do let people in, it should be based on what we actually need - but not just what businesses say they need at rock-bottom wages. If there's really a labor shortage in nursing or engineering, okay, but make sure those jobs pay enough that Americans would want them first.

*voice becoming firmer*

And here's the thing - anyone who comes needs to commit to becoming American. Learn English, follow our laws, pay taxes like everyone else. No more of this parallel society stuff where people live here for decades but never integrate. That's not fair to them or to us.

*pausing thoughtfully*

I'd also want much stronger enforcement. If someone's here illegally, they go home - no exceptions. That might sound harsh, but rules have to mean something. And employers who hire illegal workers should face real consequences, not just slaps on the wrist.

*speaking more quietly*

Look, I'm not against immigration entirely. My great-grandparents came here too. But they came when we needed them, they learned the language, they became Americans. That's the model we should go back to - controlled, legal, with real integration expected on both sides.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character10_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character10_F and your own views on immigration policy?

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character10_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
You know, for Character10_F, fairness wasn’t about everyone getting the exact same thing—it was about everybody having a real shot. She used to say, “It ain’t fair if you’re born two blocks over and suddenly you got better schools, safer streets, and folks who actually listen when you speak.” She grew up watching her mom work double shifts at the hospital laundry, coming home exhausted, barely making rent—even with a job, even with dignity. That stuck with her. Fairness meant recognizing that some people start further back, and pretending we all have equal footing just because we’re on the same map? That felt like a lie.

Belonging… that was personal. She didn’t feel fully seen a lot of the time—not by politicians, not by the news, not even by some folks in her own town who acted like lower middle class just meant “trying harder.” But she found belonging in small places: the diner where the waitress knew her order, the church basement AA meetings she went to with her uncle, the neighborhood cleanup days where people showed up with gloves and trash bags even when no one was paying them. Belonging wasn’t about fitting in perfectly—it was about being *known*, and still being welcomed.

And community? She saw it as something you build by showing up—especially when it’s hard. Not waiting for someone else to fix things. She’d say, “Community don’t mean nobody disagrees. It means we live next to each other, so we gotta figure out how to do it without hating each other.” She believed in looking out for your neighbor, even the one who drinks too much or keeps odd hours or talks different. “We’ve all got something nobody sees from the outside,” she’d say.

One time, after the snowstorm in ’22, she shoveled six driveways without being asked—including Mrs. Lin’s, the elderly Korean widow down the street who barely spoke English. When I asked why, she just said, “She’s part of this block. So she’s part of my responsibility too.” That was her—fairness as action, belonging as practice, community as something you earn every day.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character10_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*sighs softly, leaning back like she’s really seeing it*

Sitting there in the garden, dirt under my nails, sun hitting the rows of tomatoes and kale—yeah, I see them all. Maria and her kids laughing in Spanish while they water the peppers. Mr. Jenkins from two streets over, the one vets say has PTSD, quietly weeding the herb patch every morning like it’s his therapy. That young couple—bi-racial, live in the old yellow house—who got married on the porch last summer even though some folks muttered about it. And Jamal, who’s always offering to help carry tools, even though he’s still rebuilding after the overdose scare last winter.

I’ll be honest—I didn’t always know how to talk to people who didn’t grow up like me. When I first saw someone injecting insulin in broad daylight, I panicked, thought it was drugs. But then I learned. People aren’t what you assume. We’re all just trying to stay upright.

I don’t need to be best friends with everybody. But I believe in nodding. In saying good morning. In not crossing the street because someone looks or prays or loves different. Some folks worry about “losing” the neighborhood when new people move in—like culture’s a pie and if someone else gets a slice, yours shrinks. That never made sense to me. My grandma used to say, “A table gets stronger with more legs.” More voices? More ways to solve problems. More flavors in the potluck.

Yeah, sometimes there are misunderstandings. Like when the Somali family first moved in and started burning incense outside—somebody called the fire department thinking it was a blaze. Embarrassing. But we talked. They explained it was for cleansing the home. Now half the block does it during spring clean-up. Little things like that—they add up. That’s how you build something that holds.

So how do I feel? Cautious sometimes. Curious more often. And proud—proud that this messy, loud, complicated little corner of town actually *tries*. Not perfect. But trying. That’s enough for me.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Oh, absolutely. You look around and you see it—people are just *surviving*, each in their own way. I’ve got an uncle who’s been sober ten years now, but before that? Bottle every night, passed out on the couch. My mom never turned him away. She’d say, “He ain’t bad—he’s sick.” That stuck with me.

So when I see someone stumbling home late, or coughing hard from TB or whatever they’re dealing with—I don’t look away like some do. I check in. Not to fix ’em, not to judge—but just to let ’em know they’re still seen. That matters. Because shame? Shame makes everything worse. Makes people hide. And when people hide, they don’t get help.

With folks from other countries or faiths—like the Burmese family two doors down who wear different clothes, speak a language I can’t understand—I try to learn. I asked them once how to say “good morning” in their tongue. They smiled so big. Little thing. But it opened a door. Same with the gay couple raising twins—they adopted after foster care fell through. Some folks side-eye them for not being “real” parents. But I’ve seen how they show up—PTA meetings, birthday parties, fixing each other’s cars. Love’s love. Family’s family. If they’re raising kids right, loving them, contributing? Who am I to question?

But yeah—there are times we need more communication. Like when the new Haitian church started holding services outside during summer, music loud, people dancing in the street. Folks complained about noise. I get it—some of us work nights, need sleep. But instead of calling the cops, why not just talk? Sit on a porch, share a soda, explain what’s needed? Found out they didn’t know about local noise ordinances. Fixed it with a timer on the speaker. Problem solved with words, not walls.

And with disease—HIV, hepatitis, TB—fear spreads faster than germs. People whisper, avoid touching things, act like it’s punishment. That’s ignorance. I lost a friend to AIDS years ago—wasn’t some faraway thing. He was kind, funny, worked at the hardware store. Died scared because he thought no one would care. We need more honesty—education at the community center, flyers in different languages, maybe even a nurse come by once a month to answer questions. Not fear. Facts.

Tolerance isn’t about liking everything people do. It’s about respecting their right to live without being pushed out or shamed. Especially when they’re doing no harm. We all got something we’re fighting—addiction, grief, money troubles, loneliness. The least we can do is not make it harder on each other.

So yeah—I’ll talk. I’ll listen. I’ll mess up sometimes. But I won’t turn away. Because this neighborhood? It’s ours—all of ours. Even the messy parts. Especially the messy parts.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character10_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a hard one. Real hard. Because I believe in helping people—but I also remember what it felt like to stand in that unemployment line at the county office, watching jobs disappear while bills piled up. My dad lost his warehouse job when they brought in temps—cheaper, no benefits. He said they were mostly newcomers, didn’t speak much English, but would work double shifts for less. Broke him a little.

So when folks say, “Just let anyone come, we’re all human,” I get it—I do. But then I think: what about the single mom here already, working part-time at Dollar General, trying to keep the lights on? Where’s *her* fairness?

Fairness, to me, ain’t about letting everyone in or shutting everyone out. It’s about making sure the people already struggling don’t get kicked further down. If there’s only ten jobs and fifty people who need them—locals, immigrants, doesn’t matter—we can’t pretend the system’s fair just because someone’s willing to take $1 under minimum wage.

I’d want rules—fair ones. Like, if a company needs workers from outside, they should prove they tried hiring locally first. Post the job, give folks a real shot. And pay the same wages, with the same protections. No undercutting. That way, nobody’s used as a tool to drive wages into the dirt.

And I’d want support—real help—for both sides. Job training for locals who’ve been laid off. Language classes, credential recognition, legal aid for migrants so they don’t get exploited. Because when people are desperate, they’ll take anything—and that hurts everyone. Bosses start thinking, “Why pay a livable wage when I can find someone who’ll work hungry?”

I’ve seen how fear gets played too. Some politicians scream about “illegals stealing jobs” like it’s all their fault. That ain’t right. The blame’s higher up—with companies cutting corners, government not investing, schools falling apart. Migrants aren’t the enemy. They’re often running from the same kind of hardship we’d run from if our homes collapsed.

Balance? It means looking both ways. Helping my neighbor *and* the stranger—without pretending resources grow on trees. Maybe limit numbers based on what the economy can actually handle. Not shut the door, but open it slowly, fairly. With order. With dignity.

And above all—no scapegoating. We’ve got enough division. If jobs are scarce, fix the scarcity. Build more. Train more. Tax the rich who hoard billions while hospitals close. Don’t punish the person holding the shorter end of the stick just because they’re new or different.

Fairness is making sure nobody gets left behind—whether they were born here or fought to get here.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character10_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Okay, let me think… I hear all these arguments—on the news, at the diner, on Facebook rants—and honestly? Some of it hits true, some of it feels like fear dressed up as facts.

First, the good stuff: Yeah, immigrants *do* fill jobs people here won’t—or can’t—do. I’ve seen it. Who’s gonna pick strawberries for twelve hours in that heat? Who’s staffing the overnight shifts at the meatpacking plant? Not many locals. And my nurse at the clinic? From Nigeria. Best one I’ve ever had—listens, remembers my kids’ names, stays late when she doesn’t have to. So when they say we need workers, that part’s real. Labor shortages ain’t made up.

And cultural diversity? Look, I grew up eating meatloaf and mashed potatoes. Now I’ve got jerk chicken, pupusas, injera—all within walking distance. My daughter loves learning songs from other countries at school. It makes life richer. More colorful. Like someone turned on a light I didn’t know was off. That vitality? It’s not just “nice”—it’s healing. Small towns dying out? New families move in, open shops, fix up houses—that brings life back.

But then there’s the fear talk—crime, terrorism, gangs. That gets under my skin because it’s so loud. But when I actually stop and ask, “Is this true?”—I don’t see it. In our town, the immigrant families are the ones keeping their heads down, working hard, trying not to get noticed. The ones getting robbed, sometimes, because they don’t report things to police. Crime’s usually from folks already here—like that meth ring busted last year, all local boys.

Still… I can’t just dismiss the worry. I’ve sat with moms who say, “I don’t know my neighbors anymore.” Or older folks scared because they can’t understand the language at the grocery store. That loneliness? That confusion? That’s real too—even if it’s not about crime. It’s about change happening fast, and no one slowing down to help people adjust.

And yeah—humanitarian side? That matters. I’m Christian, raised to believe in loving your neighbor. If a kid’s family is fleeing bombs or starvation, how can we slam the door? My great-grandparents came from Ireland during the famine. They were called names, crowded into slums. But someone let them in. Shouldn’t we do the same?

But here’s where I struggle: the fear that wages go down, jobs disappear. And look—I’ve read enough. I know studies say immigrants don’t steal jobs overall, but *shift* them. Still, when you’re the guy not getting called back for work while temps flood in at lower pay, it *feels* personal. That pain isn’t fake, even if the big picture’s different.

So what needs more facts? The crime link. Big time. Every time someone says “immigrants are dangerous,” I want numbers. Real data. Not rumors. And terrorism? That’s such a tiny fraction—it’s used to scare people, not inform them. We need honest conversations, not headlines designed to panic.

And dialogue? We need to sit down—locals, newcomers, church leaders, workers, business owners—and just *talk*. No slogans. No politics. Just: How are you doing? What do you need? What are you afraid of?

Because fear grows in silence. And I’ve learned—whether it’s addiction, poverty, or difference—the only way through is together.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character10_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for complete openness. As much as my heart wants to say “let everyone in,” I’ve lived too close to the edge to believe we can handle unlimited numbers without breaking what little safety we’ve got. Schools overcrowded. Clinics turning people away. Rent going up because there’s more bodies than houses. I’ve seen what scarcity does—it turns neighbors against each other.

And refusing entry entirely? That’s just cruel. And short-sighted. Who’s gonna care for the elderly when our own workforce is shrinking? Who’s gonna run the farms that feed us? We need help—even if it’s hard to admit.

So what do I want?

A mix—**job-based admission**, yeah, but with *strong* rules to protect everyone. If a job’s offered, prove no local worker was available or trainable first. Pay a real wage—no undercutting. No exploiting folks who are scared to speak up. And tie work visas to labor rights, not just company profits. Because if companies can bring in workers who can’t complain, then we’re all at risk.

On top of that—**set smart numerical limits**, based on what our towns and cities can actually absorb: housing, schools, clinics, jobs. Not arbitrary cuts or floods. Something thoughtful. Like water through a filter—steady, controlled, so systems don’t collapse.

And—this is important—we **reserve part of the quota for humanitarian cases**: refugees, asylum seekers, people fleeing war or disaster. Not many—maybe 15–20%—but enough to keep our conscience clear. Because if we only let people in who “benefit the economy,” we stop being human. My grandma said, “Kindness don’t always pay the bills, but it pays something deeper.”

Also? Pathways—not just for Dreamers, but for long-term workers who’ve been here, paying taxes, raising families, staying out of trouble. Let ’em stay. Give ’em papers. Make it fair. People who’ve put years into this country shouldn’t live in fear their whole lives.

And integration support—for both sides. Fund community programs: language classes, cultural exchanges, job training. Help churches and neighborhood groups host meetups. Not forced, not preachy—just space to talk, cook together, learn. Because you don’t build trust from a distance. You build it sharing a meal, fixing a fence, helping someone’s kid with homework.

Fairness, to me, means nobody gets thrown under the bus—neither the struggling local worker afraid of losing ground, nor the migrant risking everything for a shot. Policy should protect dignity on *both* sides.

So no open borders. No closed doors. A system with heart *and* sense. That’s what I’d fight for.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character10_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character10_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. Yeah, I did.

I didn’t realize—until sitting here, speaking as her—how much of her thinking came from *witnessing* rather than judging. Not just what she believed, but *how* she believed it: rooted in what she saw with her own eyes, not what the TV or politicians said. She wasn’t academic, didn’t quote studies—but she paid attention. To people. To pain. To small acts of decency.

And I realized something about her that I hadn’t fully seen before: she carried a quiet anger—not at immigrants, but at the system that made us all compete like animals for scraps. She blamed the bosses who exploited both locals and newcomers. The politicians who stoked fear instead of fixing schools or raising wages. She didn’t want to keep people out—she wanted the game to be fair *for everyone already in it*, no matter where they started.

Embodying her made me feel how tired she was—not just physically, but morally. Tired of seeing good people suffer while powerful ones looked away. But also how stubbornly hopeful she stayed. Like, even when scared, she still chose to shovel that widow’s driveway. That wasn’t performative. It was faith—in people, in community, in doing the right thing even when it’s small.

As for me… this changed something.

I’ve always leaned more progressive than she was—wanted broader openness, faster change. But hearing her voice again—the worry in it, the protectiveness—I understand now that compassion isn’t just about welcoming others—it’s also about not abandoning the people who feel left behind. Her fears weren’t racist—they were *economic*, born from real struggle. And if we don’t acknowledge that, we lose people. We fracture.

So I see it differently now. You can’t build a just immigration policy without also building a fair economy. They’re tied. One without the other? That breeds resentment. That breaks communities.

She reminded me that policy isn’t just ideas on paper—it’s about faces. The woman working three jobs. The teenager fleeing violence. The old man afraid his town doesn’t feel like home anymore.

You don’t honor Character10_F by forgetting her concerns—or by dismissing them. You honor her by holding them alongside the bigger picture. By trying to care about *all* the neighbors.

And yeah… I miss her. But today, I felt her here. Like she was still trying to teach me something.
